runs.text: How does a CDN make websites faster?

script.title: How a CDN makes websites faster

beats.say: A user opens their browser to visit a website.
Without a CDN, every request travels to the origin server, often across continents.
This is the slow path: high latency, slow load times.
With a CDN, the browser hits a nearby edge server instead.
The edge checks its cache. A hit serves instantly.
On a miss, the edge fetches once, then caches for the next user.
Result: shorter trips, less load on origin, faster pages for everyone.

beats.say: Your code runs on the call stack first.
Slow tasks get offloaded to Web APIs like timers or fetch.
When done, their callbacks move to the task queue.
The event loop waits, then pushes callbacks back to the stack when it's clear.
This cycle keeps JavaScript non-blocking and responsive.

runs.text: How does Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm work?

beats.say: Start at the source node with tentative distances set to infinity, except zero for itself.
Pick the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance.
For each neighbor, update their distance if a shorter path is found through the current node.
Mark the current node as visited; its shortest path is now confirmed.
Check if any unvisited nodes remain to continue processing.
Loop back to pick the next minimum from remaining unvisited nodes.
When all nodes are visited, the algorithm finishes with shortest paths found.

Finally, a Running process exits and becomes Terminated, ending its lifecycle.
